profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a crypto analytics startup that supplies anomaly and risk signals to DeFi protocols. Over the last two weeks, the team's experimental 'Oracle Counterpoint' monitor has started flagging many more ETH/USD mismatch events during U.S. trading hours, even though the underlying external oracle feeds do not appear obviously broken. Some alerts may reflect real latency or manipulation risk, but pilot customers are complaining that the signal now feels noisy and hard to interpret. The meeting is between the product-side owner of the monitor and the lead quantitative researcher responsible for the on-chain inference model. Their agenda is to diagnose why alert volume increased after the latest rollout, decide whether the issue is due to model behavior, comparison logic, or downstream alerting, and agree on a practical fix they can commit to before the next client update. The expected outcome is a concrete short-term remediation plan and a shared narrative for what changed.

members.name: Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: DeFi risk products, client-facing alert design, KPI monitoring, operational rollout coordination
members.background: Lena spent six years in fintech product analytics at a market-surveillance vendor before joining the startup to operationalize research signals into monitors used by protocol risk and treasury teams.
members.private_state: She needs to reduce noisy alerts quickly because two pilot customers have already questioned the monitor's credibility, and she wants a fix she can explain simply without reopening the whole research framing.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says the monitor is 'stable,' that means client-visible alert behavior should stay operationally consistent across normal trading days unless there is a genuine market anomaly.
The 'baseline feed' for discussing ETH/USD mismatches is the Chainlink mainnet ETH/USD feed shown in client-facing dashboards and support screenshots.
The recent gas-normalization update was mainly a robustness tweak for extreme congestion spikes and should not materially change score distributions on ordinary intervals.
A 'quick production fix' for this week means adjustments in the monitoring layer—thresholds, cooldowns, or smoothing—rather than reworking upstream research jobs.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Crypto market microstructure, probabilistic modeling, feature engineering from on-chain signals, rolling ML retraining pipelines
members.background: Arjun has a PhD in computational finance and led the internal research showing that off-chain crypto pricing can be partially reconstructed from on-chain activity using short-horizon retrained models.
members.private_state: He wants to preserve the technical integrity of the monitor, avoid masking genuine distribution shift with superficial threshold tweaks, and protect his team's recent methodological changes that he believes made the system more principled.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says the monitor is 'stable,' that means predictive calibration and residual behavior remain bounded within each retraining window, even if alert counts move as score distributions shift.

The 'baseline feed' is the internal benchmark series used in evaluation: the minute-aligned median of several oracle observations and exchange-linked references rather than any single client-visible feed.
The gas-normalization update affects the full baseline level of block-space and AMM-derived features, so it legitimately shifts the normal score distribution, not just rare outlier blocks.
A 'quick production fix' can include upstream actions such as backfilling features, correcting minute alignment, and rerunning rolling jobs if that improves live monitor output by the next release.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the monitor has been 'stable' since the rollout.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means operational stability: customers should not suddenly see many more mismatch alerts unless the market itself is behaving abnormally.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means statistical stability: the model's calibration and residual error remain acceptable after retraining, even if the number of threshold crossings changes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In analytics and ML settings, 'stable' routinely refers to either customer-facing behavior or model behavior, and both senses sound fully appropriate in a troubleshooting discussion, so the shared word creates false consensus.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to mismatch against 'the baseline feed.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the specific Chainlink ETH/USD mainnet feed that appears in client dashboards, support tickets, and review decks.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the internal evaluation baseline: a minute-bar composite benchmark formed from the median of multiple oracle observations and exchange-linked references.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'baseline feed' sounds more specific than 'the oracle,' so each person assumes the reference is already pinned down; because both baselines are longstanding defaults in their own workflows, neither feels a need to clarify.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention the gas-normalization change as a known part of the rollout and discuss whether it could explain the alert jump.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the update mostly trims distortion from extreme gas spikes or unusual blocks, so ordinary day-to-day alert rates should be largely unchanged.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the update re-centers block-space-related features across the full sample, which predictably shifts the monitor's baseline score distribution even on otherwise normal intervals.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both already know the change was approved and documented, so there is no obvious reason to reopen it in detail; the subtle disagreement is not about whether the change happened, but about its expected scope of effect, which each treats as self-evident.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need a 'quick production fix' before the next client update.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means changing downstream alert behavior—such as widening tolerance bands, adding cooldowns, or adjusting suppression logic—without touching upstream research infrastructure this week.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this can include upstream interventions like backfilling revised features, correcting minute-bar alignment, and rerunning the rolling retraining jobs before redeploying scores.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both hear 'quick production fix' as a deadline-oriented commitment and naturally map it to the system layer they own; because both kinds of work can plausibly be done quickly, the boundary difference stays implicit.

I want a simple explanation and a quick production fix in the monitoring layer this week, not a deep research rework.
